title: The alphabet and the vowels
description: Letter names, the five vowels, and why Italian spelling is so regular.
objectives: Name the 21 letters of the Italian alphabet and recognise the 5 foreign letters.
Pronounce the five vowels as pure, unreduced sounds.
Understand that final vowels carry grammatical information (gender and number).
Know that h is always silent.

blocks.text: The native Italian alphabet has 21 letters. Five more — *j, k, w, x, y* — occur only in loanwords and foreign names (*il jazz, il kiwi, il weekend, lo yogurt*).
Foreign letters: *j* (i lunga), *k* (cappa), *w* (doppia vu), *x* (ics), *y* (ipsilon or i greca).

blocks.title: The letter h is always silent
blocks.text: *h* is never pronounced. It has two jobs: inside *ch* and *gh* it keeps *c* and *g* hard (see the next lesson), and at the start of four forms of *avere* — *ho, hai, ha, hanno* — it distinguishes them in writing from *o* (or), *ai* (to the), *a* (to) and *anno* (year).
Italian has five vowel letters: *a, e, i, o, u*. Each is pronounced fully and clearly, whether stressed or not. English often weakens unstressed vowels to a neutral 'uh' sound; Italian never does.

blocks.caption: Approximate vowel sounds
rows: the e in bed (open) or a closed 'ay' without the glide
the ee in see, but short
the o in for (open) or a pure closed 'oh'
the oo in moon, but short

blocks.title: Open and closed e and o
blocks.text: Stressed *e* and *o* can be open or closed (*bène* versus *séra*; *còsa* versus *sóle*). Standard Italian therefore has seven stressed vowel sounds: a, è [ɛ], é [e], i, ò [ɔ], ó [o], u. In unstressed syllables only five occur. The distribution of open and closed vowels follows Florentine usage in the standard, but it varies a great deal by region (many speakers in the North and South distribute them differently), and only a few word pairs depend on it (*pèsca* 'peach' / *pésca* 'fishing'; *vènti* 'winds' / *vénti* 'twenty'). A regional distribution is not an error in everyday speech; dictionaries mark the standard one with grave (è, ò) and acute (é, ó) accents, and you can check any word there.

blocks.title: Final vowels matter
blocks.text: Many words differ only in their final vowel: *gatto* (cat) and *gatti* (cats); *bambino* (boy) and *bambina* (girl). The final vowel often marks gender and number, so it must be pronounced clearly.

Italian spelling is highly regular: once you know a handful of rules (mostly about *c*, *g*, *sc*, *gn* and *gli*), you can pronounce almost any written word correctly, and spell almost any word you hear.

items: Every written vowel is pronounced: *idea* has three syllables (i-de-a), *aereo* has four (a-e-re-o).
*z* sounds like ts or dz: *zio* (tsio), *zaino* (dzaino) — the choice varies by word and region.

examples.note: ho: the h is silent — pronounced 'o'.
Only the final vowel (and the article) changes.

exercises.prompt: How is the h in *ho* (I have) pronounced?
options: Like the ch in Scottish loch
exercises.explanation: h is never pronounced in Italian. ho sounds exactly like o (or); the h only distinguishes the two in writing.

exercises.prompt: Match each letter to its Italian name.
exercises.explanation: Consonant names follow two patterns: vowel + consonant + e (effe, elle, emme, enne, erre, esse) or consonant + i (bi, ci, di, gi, pi, ti). h (acca), q (cu) and z (zeta) are special.

exercises.prompt: Which of these letters appears only in loanwords?
exercises.explanation: j, k, w, x and y are not part of the native Italian alphabet; they appear in words such as il kiwi or il weekend.

exercises.prompt: *gatto* and *gatti* differ only in the final vowel. What does that vowel show here?
exercises.explanation: gatto = cat, gatti = cats. Final vowels carry gender and number, which is why they are always pronounced clearly.
Every Italian vowel is pronounced: i-de-a.
bambina ends in -a: a girl. bambino (-o) is a boy.

summary: 21 native letters; j, k, w, x, y only in loanwords.
Five pure vowels, always fully pronounced — including at the end of words.
Spelling is regular: learn the few rules for c, g, sc, gn, gli and you can read aloud almost anything.

title: Hard and soft c and g; sc, gn and gli
description: When c and g are hard or soft, the role of h and i, and the sounds sc, gn and gli.
objectives: Predict whether c and g are hard (k, g) or soft (ch, j) from the following letter.
Use ch/gh and ci/gi spellings correctly.
Pronounce sc, gn, gli and qu.

sections.heading: c and g before different vowels

blocks.title: The basic rule
blocks.text: Before *a, o, u* (and consonants), *c* and *g* are **hard**: c = k, g = g as in 'go'. Before *e, i* they are **soft**: c = ch as in 'church', g = j as in 'jam'.

blocks.title: h makes c and g hard before e and i
blocks.text: To write the hard sound before *e* or *i*, insert *h*: *che* (ke), *chi* (ki), *ghe*, *ghi*. This is why the plural of *lago* is *laghi* and *tu cerchi* is spelt with h.

blocks.title: i makes c and g soft before a, o, u
blocks.text: To write the soft sound before *a, o, u*, insert an *i* that is not pronounced as a separate vowel: *ciao* (chao), *giallo* (jallo), *mangio* (manjo).
The same logic as c: h keeps it hard, i keeps it soft. That is why *uscire* has the forms *esco* (sk) and *esci* (sh).

items: *gn* = the ny sound of Spanish ñ or the ni in 'onion': *montagna, sogno, bagno*.
*gli* = a palatal l, close to the lli in 'million': *famiglia, figlio, foglia, coniglio*. Before *a, o, u* the i is not pronounced separately: *foglia* = fo-lya.
*qu* = kw: *quando, quattro, questo*. The u is always pronounced.

blocks.title: A few hard gl words
blocks.text: In a small number of learned words *gl* + i is pronounced g + l, as in English: *glicine* (wisteria), *glicerina, glifo, anglicano, negligente* and some proper names. (*globo* is hard simply because gl is followed by o, not i.) They are few, and a dictionary shows the pronunciation.

examples.note: ciao: soft c, the i is silent.

examples.it: La mia famiglia vive in montagna.
examples.en: My family lives in the mountains.

exercises.prompt: In which word is c pronounced like English k?
exercises.explanation: ch before i or e is hard (k). In cena and cielo the c is soft before e/i, and in ciao the i signals a soft c before a.

exercises.prompt: In which word is g pronounced like the j in 'jam'?
exercises.explanation: gi before o = soft g. gatto and gufo have g before a/u (hard); laghi uses gh to keep g hard before i.

exercises.prompt: *il lago* (the lake) becomes plural. Which spelling keeps the hard g sound?
exercises.explanation: Plural -i would make g soft (lagi = laji). The h keeps the hard sound: laghi.

mistakes.message: lagi would be pronounced 'laji'. Insert h to keep g hard before i: laghi.

exercises.prompt: Match each word to its sound.
exercises.explanation: sc + u = sk; sc + e = sh; gn = ny; gli = palatal l.

exercises.prompt: Complete the spellings to match the sounds given in brackets.
exercises.explanation: chiave (ch = k before i), giallo (gi = j before a), scuola (sc = sk before u), scherzo (sch = sk before e).

exercises.prompt: How do you pronounce the *u* in *quando*?
options: As oo in a separate syllable: ku-an-do
exercises.explanation: After q, u is always pronounced as a w sound.

summary: c, g, sc are hard before a, o, u and soft before e, i.
Insert h to keep them hard before e/i (che, laghi, scherzo).
Insert a silent i to make them soft before a/o/u (ciao, giallo, sciarpa).
gn = ny, gli = palatal l, qu = kw.

title: Syllables, stress, double consonants and accents
description: Where the stress falls, why double consonants matter, when accents are written, and elision with the apostrophe.
objectives: Divide words into syllables and locate the stress.
Pronounce and spell double consonants and recognise minimal pairs.
Know when an accent must be written, and the difference between è and e.
Use the apostrophe for elision (l'albero, un'amica, c'è).

blocks.text: Italian syllables tend to end in a vowel: *ca-sa, ma-ti-ta, fi-ne-stra*. A double consonant is split between two syllables (*gat-to, mam-ma*), and *s* + consonant goes with the following syllable (*pa-sta, fi-ne-stra*).

blocks.title: Stress usually falls on the second-to-last syllable
blocks.text: Most words are stressed on the penultimate syllable: *CA-sa, bam-BI-no, fi-NE-stra*. Many common words, however, are stressed on the third-to-last: *AL-be-ro, TA-vo-lo, MAC-chi-na, PEC-co-ra*. This is not shown in writing, so learn the stress with each new word.

blocks.title: Final stress is always written
blocks.text: If the stress falls on the last vowel of a word of two or more syllables, it is always marked with an accent: *città, caffè, perché, papà, più, felicità*.
Italian writes a grave accent (à, è, ì, ò, ù) on most stressed final vowels. A small set of words take an acute accent on closed *é*: *perché, poiché, né, sé*, and compounds like *ventitré*.

blocks.caption: One-syllable words distinguished only by the accent

blocks.title: Never write e' for è
blocks.text: The apostrophe is not an accent. Writing *e'* for *è* is a typing habit, not standard spelling. In this course an answer without the correct accent is marked wrong.

blocks.title: Double consonants are held longer
blocks.text: A written double consonant is pronounced longer (or with more tension) than a single one. The difference can change meaning entirely.
When certain short words end in a vowel and the next word begins with a vowel, the first vowel is dropped and replaced by an apostrophe, with no space after it.

blocks.title: un amico — no apostrophe
blocks.text: The masculine *un* is not an elided form (it is also used before consonants: *un gatto*), so it never takes an apostrophe: *un amico*, but *un'amica*. Likewise *qual è* is written without an apostrophe.

examples.note: l' (from lo) before a vowel; AL-be-ro is stressed on the third-to-last syllable.
nonno: double n. caffè: written final stress.
è (is) carries an accent; e (and) does not.

examples.en: There is a bee on the flower.
examples.note: c'è = ci + è; un'ape = una + ape.

exercises.prompt: Write the missing word meaning 'is': Il gatto ___ nero.
exercises.explanation: è (with an accent) is the verb 'is'. e without an accent means 'and'.

mistakes.message: Without the accent, e means 'and'. 'Is' is è.
An apostrophe is not an accent: write è.

exercises.explanation: nonno (double n) = grandfather; nono (single n) = ninth.
una elides to un' before a vowel, with no space: un'amica. Without the apostrophe (un amica) it would be the masculine form.
Masculine un never takes an apostrophe: un amico, un albero.

mistakes.message: Only the feminine una is elided (un'amica). Masculine un never takes an apostrophe.

exercises.prompt: Which word is stressed on the third-to-last syllable?
exercises.explanation: AL-be-ro. bam-BI-no and fi-NE-stra follow the usual penultimate stress; cit-TÀ has written final stress.

exercises.text: {0}acqua (the water) · {1} un orso (there is a bear) · {2} la mamma? (where is Mum?)
exercises.explanation: la → l' before a vowel; ci + è → c'è; dove + è → dov'è.

summary: Stress usually falls on the second-to-last syllable, but many words are stressed earlier — learn it with the word.
Final stress is always written: città, caffè, perché.
Accents distinguish è/e, là/la, sì/si, dà/da, tè/te.
Double consonants are pronounced longer and can change meaning.
Elision: l'albero, un'amica, c'è — but un amico.
